______________________________________________________________________

REASONS OF JUSTICE MORIN

___________________________________________________________________

[
5
]

The appellants reside in two buildings that form
part of a luxury residential complex known as "Le Sanctuaire du
Mont-Royal", in the city of Montréal. These two buildings, constructed in phases VI and VII of the
residential development, are known as "Place Northcrest". They are
subject to a declaration of divided co-ownership, and the co-owners in the two
buildings together constitute a single syndicate, the respondent in this
appeal.

[
6
]

The appellants claim that the trial judge erred
in allowing the respondent's action for permanent injunction against them and
the two mis en cause, Miguel Bernfield and Edith Jaul, and in ordering all of
these persons:

1 – to refrain
from erecting any shelter, structure, construction or "succah" on the
common portions reserved for exclusive use of the co-owned property located at
6300-6301 Place Northcrest, in Montréal;

2 – to proceed
immediately with the demolition or dismantling of any shelters, structures or
"succahs" installed on the common portions reserved for exclusive
use, if applicable.

3 – to restore
immediately the balconies, patios or terraces of the co-owned property to their
original state, at their own costs.

[
7
]

I do not believe it is necessary to recite all
the facts and the proceedings arising from this, as the trial judge has
accomplished this task admirably.
[1]

[
8
]

It is sufficient to point out simply that the
dispute between the parties arises from the fact that, in the fall of 1997, the
appellants and the two mis en cause erected a "succah" on the balcony
or terrace adjoining their respective residential units to celebrate the Jewish
holiday of Succot, despite the objections of the respondent.
[2]
The trial judge summarized the link between
this holiday and the building of succahs in the following terms:

[
translation
]

To celebrate this holiday,
practising Jews must, for a period of eight days beginning at sunset on the
first day, dwell in a succah, that is, a rough structure made of wood or canvas
with an open roof covered with only fir branches or bamboo, as the roof must for
the most part remain open to the sky.
[3]

[
9
]

I should add that, pursuant to the declaration
of co-ownership, balconies and terraces are not private portions, but common
portions reserved for the exclusive use of the owners of the apartments
adjacent to them.

[
10
]

Such being the case, the questions raised in the
present case must be defined clearly at the outset. Accordingly, in the
prologue to his judgment, the trial judge provided a lucid outline of the
issues:

[
translation
]

Three sources of law govern the
contractual relations between individuals: the
Civil Code of Québec

(S.Q. 1991, c. 64), the
Charter of human rights and freedoms
(R.S.Q., c.
C-12, hereinafter the
Charter
), and the general principles of law. This
is the fundamental rule set out in the sole preliminary provision of the
Civil
Code of Québec
.

Applying these rules harmoniously
is a task not without its own difficulties in cases where the collective rights
of co-owners conflict with the individual freedom of religion of some within
the group.

The present dispute crystallizes
the difficulties inherent in maintaining this crucial harmony.

The four days of hearing have been
devoted to finding answers to the following questions:

1.

What are the restrictions set out in the
co-ownership agreement?

2.

Are these restrictions justified by the
destination, characteristics or location of the immovable?

3.

Do these restrictions infringe on the freedom of
religion of the respondents or violate their equality rights?

4.

If so, did the respondent offer reasonable
accommodation to correct this inequality?

5.

If so, is the violation justified under
section
9.1
of the
Charter
?

6.

In the absence of serious and irreparable
prejudice, may a co-owner be compelled to comply with the declaration of
co-ownership (art. 1080 C.C.Q.)?
[4]

Restrictions imposed by the
co-ownership agreement

[
11
]

The trial judge responded to the first of these
six questions in the following manner:

[
translation
]

The restrictions imposed on the
rights of the co-owners are found essentially in clauses 2.6.3, 6.5, 6.16 and 9.3
of the declaration of co-ownership. They read as follows:

[
translation
]

2.6.3 Balconies,
porches and patios

The owner of each exclusive portion
(dwelling unit) with a door leading to a balcony, porch or patio adjoining his
or her exclusive portion (dwelling unit) has the personal and exclusive use of
the balcony, or of the portion of the porch adjoining his or her exclusive
portion, subject to the following rules:

(a)

On porches, an area at least as wide as is required under fire
safety by-laws must be kept free of garden furniture and other accessories, as
the porches serve as emergency exits.

(b)

No owner may enclose or block off any balcony, porch or patio in any
manner whatsoever or erect thereon constructions of any kind whatsoever.

(c)

Balconies constructed on terraces or patios are reserved for the
private and exclusive use of the owner of each exclusive portion (dwelling
unit) with a door leading to the above-mentioned balcony or patio, but the
maintenance of these terraces or patios (including the mowing of lawns) is a
common duty.

…

6.5
Uniformity
of décor in the building

Entrance doors to the exclusive
portions (dwelling units), windows, painted exterior surfaces and,
in
general, any exterior elements contributing to the overall harmony of the
building's appearance may under no circumstances be altered, even if they are
part of the limited common portions
, without first obtaining the written
permission of the Board of Directors, who themselves must first obtain the
approval of the co-owners at a general meeting.

6.16
Exterior
decorations prohibited

Co-owners may not decorate, paint
or alter the exterior of the exclusive portions in any way whatsoever without
first obtaining the written consent of the Board of Directors, subject to any
exceptions provided for in this declaration.

9.3

Balconies and porches

Subject to the law and to this
declaration, each co-owner having exclusive use of a balcony or a portion of a
porch adjoining his or her exclusive portion (dwelling unit), as provided for
in clause 2.6.3, shall keep said balcony or portion of the porch clean. The
co-owner having exclusive use of said balcony or portion of the porch is solely
responsible for the day-to-day maintenance thereof. However, the Board of
Directors is responsible for the replacement of or repairs to said balconies
and porches as a common expense, unless the balcony or porch must be repaired
or replaced because of the fault or negligence of a co-owner or someone for
whom that co-owner is legally responsible, in which case the costs and expenses
of any repairs or replacement shall be assumed by the co-owner in question.

Furthermore, subject to acts and
regulations of general application,
nothing other than usual outdoor
furniture may be left or stored on a balcony or porch
without first obtaining
permission in writing from the Board of Directors. Under no circumstances may
balconies or porches be used for drying laundry, towels, etc.

No balcony or porch may be
decorated, covered, enclosed or painted in any way whatsoever without the prior
written permission
of the co-owners or the Board of
Directors, as the case may be.
[5]

[Emphasis added.]

[
12
]

After analyzing the various clauses of the
declaration of co-ownership, the judge concluded the following:

[
translation
]

On reading all the clauses containing
restrictions, the Court quickly concludes that the erection of succahs is
prohibited. Whether or not the succah is considered a construction is of little
consequence. Enclosing, blocking off or decorating a balcony or patio in any
way whatsoever is prohibited. In short, apart from the usual outdoor furniture,
owners may not make any alterations to the exterior. They may not place
anything whatsoever outside. When considered as a whole, these restrictions
demonstrate a clear intent to maintain the original condition and uniform
appearance of the building's exterior.
[6]

[
13
]

The appellants maintain that the trial judge
erred in reaching the above-noted conclusion. They rely,
inter alia
, on
semantic arguments, claiming that a succah cannot be considered a construction,
alteration or decoration. They also affirm that clauses 6.5 and 6.16 apply only
to exclusive portions and not to the common portions reserved for the exclusive
use of a co-owner, such as balconies and terraces.

[
14
]

In this respect, the appellants' interpretation
of the above-cited clauses of the declaration of co-ownership amounts to
nit-picking. They become caught up in so many details that they overlook the
general import of the declaration. In so doing, they fail to comply with

articles 1425
to
1427
of the
Civil Code of Québec
, which state the
following:

1425.
The common intention of the parties rather than adherence to the literal
meaning of the words shall be sought in interpreting a contract.

1426.
In interpreting a contract, the nature of the contract, the circumstances
in which it was formed, the interpretation which has already been given to it
by the parties or which it may have received, and usage, are all taken into
account.

1427.
Each clause of a contract is interpreted in light of the others so that
each is given the meaning derived from the contract as a whole.

[
15
]

The trial judge considered the relevant clauses
of the declaration of co-ownership as a whole in light of these statutory
provisions, and, based on the evidence before him, correctly concluded that
these clauses prohibit the construction of succahs on balconies and terraces.

The restrictions and the destination of
the immovable

[
16
]

Having thus answered the first question, I now
move on to the second: are the restrictions imposed by the declaration of
co-ownership justified in light of
article 1056
of the
Civil Code of Québec
?

1056. No declaration of
co-ownership may impose any restriction on the rights of the co-owners except
restrictions justified by the destination, characteristics or location of the
immovable.

[
17
]

The trial judge undertook a thorough analysis of
this question, providing a two-part answer under the following headings:

[
translation
]

1.

Are the restrictions justified?
[7]

2.

The act constituting the co-ownership.
[8]

[
18
]

The judge notes that the immovables that make up
Place Northcrest are upscale buildings and that the co-owners have a marked
interest in preserving their harmony and aesthetic value. In particular, he
notes that the act constituting the co-ownership was drafted in such a way that
the balconies and terraces remain the common property of all the co-owners
precisely to ensure their preservation.

[
19
]

Following this analysis, the judge concludes:

[
translation
]

To sum up, on this first point the
Court finds that the restrictions imposed on the co-owners were in compliance
with the applicable principles specified in
article 1056
C.C.Q. The Court also
finds that over time, the syndicate interpreted and applied these restrictions
in a uniform manner, in compliance with the content of the restrictions. The
respondents cannot claim that they have been denied a right which was granted
the other owners.
[9]

[
20
]

The appellants
maintain that, in reaching this conclusion, the trial judge erred in
his assessment of the evidence, and they invite the Court to
substitute its own assessment and thereby arrive at a totally different
conclusion. In my view, the trial judge committed no error in assessing the
evidence. I therefore do not believe that there is any reason for this Court to
repeat the exercise and substitute its own assessment for that of the trial
judge.

[
21
]

In addition, I am of the view that the judge
correctly directed himself in law on the basis of his findings of fact. In the
circumstances, I believe that he was justified in concluding that the
restrictions imposed on the co-owners pursuant to the clauses of the
declaration of co-ownership were in compliance with
article 1056
of the
Civil
Code of Québec
.

[
22
]

At this point it is appropriate to note that in
Kilzi

v. Syndicat des copropriétaires du 10,400 boulevard l'Acadie
, this Court
recommended the adoption of a [
translation
]

"broader"
notion of the destination
of the immovable:

[
translation
]

This interpretation complies with
that advocated in the preliminary drafts of the French act, which was the
inspiration for our own legislation. The definition suggested therein reads as
follows:

[
translation
]

All of the conditions
subject to which co-owners purchased their lot, considered in light of various
factors, in particular, of all of the clauses, the contractual documents, the
physical characteristics and location of the immovable, and the social
circumstances of the occupants.
[10]

[
23
]

This is the interpretation the trial judge
applied in reaching the above-noted conclusion.

Freedom of religion

[
24
]

Having dealt with this question, the trial judge
then turned to the central issue in the present dispute, namely, freedom of
religion, by responding to the third, fourth and fifth questions he had set out
on this matter.

[
25
]

The trial judge carried out a very thorough
study of the question of freedom of religion, examining the notion of freedom
of religion itself, its practical implementation, the duty to accommodate that
may arise in certain circumstances, and finally the application of
section 9.1

of the
Quebec
Charter of human rights and freedoms
, which states the
following:

9.1

In exercising his fundamental freedoms and rights, a person shall maintain a
proper regard for democratic values, public order and the general well-being of
the citizens of Québec.

In this respect, the scope of the
freedoms and rights, and limits to their exercise, may be fixed by law.

[
26
]

Although I recognize the effort the trial judge
invested in his analysis, I find that his interpretation of the notion of
freedom of religion is too restrictive. He began with the following remark:

[
translation
]

This leads us to the delicate
question of what the higher courts have called the "inquiry into the
sincerity of the religious belief". This rule requires seeking the content
of the religious obligation, which alone can be protected.
[11]

[
27
]

Later, returning to this idea, he stated:

[
translation
]

"Sincerity of religious
belief" is perhaps not the most accurate of terms. Rather, the inquiry
must centre on the teaching of religious precepts and their obligatory content.
[12]

[
28
]

Finally, he summed up his reasoning in the
following manner:

[
translation
]

To sum up, freedom of religion can
be relied on only if there is a connection between the right asserted by a
person to practise his or her religion in a given way and what is considered
mandatory pursuant to the religious teaching upon which the right is based. To
be sincere, a belief must be supported by the existence of a religious precept.
How the teaching is observed may vary and may not necessarily correspond to how
most believers perform their religious obligations. Nonetheless, the rite must
have a rational, reasonable and direct connection with the teaching. How a
believer fulfils his or her religious obligations cannot be grounded in a
purely subjective personal understanding that bears no relation to the
religious teaching as regards both the belief itself and how the belief is to
be expressed (the rite).
[13]

[
29
]

The trial judge then reviewed the evidence
presented before him, in particular the testimony of the two experts, Rabbi
Barry Levy and Rabbi Moïse Ohana, and arrived at the following conclusion:

[
translation
]

First of all, the court notes that
practising Jews are not under a religious obligation to erect their own
succahs. There is no commandment as to where they must be erected.
[14]

[
30
]

He provides additional reasons further on,
stating the following:

[
translation
]

Like a religious obligation or
commandment, a religious rite is imposed through religious teaching and/or
interpretation by religious authority. These elements are external to the
believer. We may not properly speak of the "sincerity of the belief"
based on an individual and therefore subjective concept. To adopt such an
approach would inevitably lead to situations beyond any control, where freedom
of religion would be replaced with the freedom of each individual to do
anything at all in the name of his or her own concepts of religion and
religious rites.
[15]

[
31
]

In reaching these various conclusions, the trial
judge appears to depart from the interpretation of the very notion of freedom
of religion that was adopted by the Supreme Court of Canada and expressed by
Justice Dickson in
R. v. Big M Drug Mart Ltd
.:

The essence of the
concept of freedom of religion is the right to entertain such religious beliefs
as a person chooses, the right to declare religious beliefs openly and without
fear of hindrance or reprisal, and the right to manifest religious belief by
worship and practice or by teaching and dissemination. But the concept means
more than that.

Freedom can primarily
be characterized by the absence of coercion or constraint. If a person is
compelled by the state or the will of another to a course of action or inaction
which he would not otherwise have chosen, he is not acting of his own volition
and he cannot be said to be truly free. One of the major purposes of the
Charter

is to protect, within reason, from compulsion or restraint. Coercion includes
not only such blatant forms of compulsion as direct commands to act or refrain
from acting on pain of sanction, coercion includes indirect forms of control
which determine or limit alternative courses of conduct available to others.
Freedom in a broad sense embraces both the absence of coercion and constraint,
and the right to manifest beliefs and practices. Freedom means that, subject to
such limitations as are necessary to protect public safety, order, health, or
morals or the fundamental rights and freedoms of others, no one is to be forced
to act in a way contrary to his beliefs or his conscience.
[16]

[
32
]

As that case instructs, it is the sincerity of
the belief dictated by the individual's conscience that must be considered when
freedom of religion is relied upon to justify an act or a refusal to act. It
matters little that those beliefs may be erroneous if judged according to the
official teachings of the leaders of the religious community to which the
individual belongs. The trial judge came to the opposite conclusion, as already
noted.

[
33
]

The evidence shows that the appellants have a
sincere belief, based specifically on chapter 8, verses 13 to 18 of the Book of
Nehemiah in the Bible, that they must erect their own succahs and dwell in them
for several days during the festival of Succot. In theory, the principle of
freedom of religion should protect their right to do so. In practice, however,
the above-quoted clauses of the declaration of co-ownership prevent them from
doing as they wish by banning the erection of succahs on the balconies or
terraces adjoining their dwelling units.

[
34
]

These clauses therefore infringe on their
freedom of religion, expressly recognized in
section 3
of the
Charter of
human rights and freedoms
:

3.
Every person is the possessor of the
fundamental freedoms, including freedom of conscience, freedom of religion,
freedom of opinion, freedom of expression, freedom of peaceful assembly and
freedom of association.

[
35
]

The trial judge arrived at the contrary
conclusion, although he did not stop there, adding the following:

[
translation
]

The Court is not satisfied that the
restrictions on the rights of co-ownership infringe on the respondent's freedom
of religion since these restrictions do not prevent the respondents from
performing their religious obligations. Because this is a delicate question,
however, it is appropriate to take the analysis one step further and speculate
on the outcome of this dispute if the Court had accepted the opposing argument,
that is, that there had been an infringement of the freedom of religion.

To do so, we must answer two
subsidiary questions: if there were an infringement on the freedom of religion
as a consequence of the harmful effects of the enforcement of the contract, has
the claimant met its duty to accommodate and, second, can this infringement be
justified under
section 9.1
of the
Charter
?
[17]

Restrictions and freedom of religion

[
36
]

The trial judge then turned his attention to the
fourth and fifth questions set out at the beginning of his reasons. In my
opinion, he correctly directed himself in law by drawing a distinction between
direct discrimination and adverse effect discrimination, according to the state
of the law on the date of the trial judgment, June 5, 1998.

[
37
]

Since then, however, the state of the law on
such matters has been modified by the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada
in
British Columbia (Public Service Employee Relations Commission) v. BCGSEU
,

handed down on September 9, 1999
.
[18]

[
38
]

Given the importance of that decision in the
analysis of the present matter, it is useful to cite extensive excerpts from
it.

[
39
]

First of all, in the introduction to the
judgment, Justice McLachlin summarizes the issue before the Court:

Seven years ago
Tawney Meiorin was hired as a forest firefighter by the Province of British
Columbia (the "Government"). Although she did her work well, she lost
her job three years later when the Government adopted a new series of fitness
tests for forest firefighters. She passed three of the tests but failed a
fourth one, a 2.5 kilometre run designed to assess whether she met the
Government's aerobic standard, by taking 49.4 seconds longer than required.

The narrow issue in
this case is whether the Government improperly dismissed Ms. Meiorin from her
job as a forest firefighter. The broader legal issue is whether the aerobic
standard that led to Ms. Meiorin's dismissal unfairly excludes women from forest
firefighting jobs. Employers seeking to maintain safety may err on the side of
caution and set standards higher than are necessary for the safe performance of
the work. However, if men and women do not have an equal ability to meet the
excessive standard, the effect may be to exclude qualified female candidates
from employment for no reason but their gender. Like human rights legislation
throughout Canada, the
British Columbia
Human Rights Code
,
R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 210, seeks
to counter this by requiring employers to justify their standards where
prima
facie
discrimination is established. The question in this case is whether
the Government has done so.

Although this case
may be resolved on the basis of the conventional bifurcated analysis this Court
has applied to claims of workplace discrimination under human rights statutes,
the parties have invited us to reconsider that approach. Accepting this
invitation, I propose a revised approach to what an employer must show to
justify a
prima facie
case of discrimination. On this approach, I
conclude that Ms. Meiorin has demonstrated that the Government's aerobic
standard is
prima facie
discriminatory and the Government has failed to
establish on the record before this Court that it is a
bona fide

occupational requirement ("BFOR"). I would therefore allow the appeal
and restore the arbitrator's decision to reinstate Ms. Meiorin.
[19]

[
40
]

After this introduction, Justice McLachlin
summarizes the facts, the decisions appealed from, and the applicable
legislation, specifically,
sections 13(1)
and
13(4)
of the
British Columbia
Human
Rights Code
, which read as follows:

13
(1) A person must not

(a)

refuse to employ or refuse to continue to employ a person, or

(b)

discriminate against a person regarding employment or any term or
condition of employment

because of the race, colour,
ancestry, place of origin, political belief, religion, marital status, family
status, physical or mental disability, sex, sexual orientation or age of that
person or because that person has been convicted of a criminal or summary
conviction offence that is unrelated to the employment or to the intended
employment of that person.

…

(4) Subsections (1) and (2) do not
apply with respect to a refusal, limitation, specification or preference based
on a bona fide occupational requirement.
[20]

[
41
]

She then describes the questions at issue in the
following terms:

The first issue on
this appeal is the test applicable to
s.13(1)
and
(4)
of the
British Columbia
Human
Rights Code
. The second issue is whether, on this test, Ms. Meiorin has
established that the Government violated the Code.
[21]

[
42
]

Justice McLachlin then describes the
conventional approach that had until then been used to deal with questions such
as the one at issue in the appeal:

The conventional
approach to applying human rights legislation in the workplace requires the
tribunal to decide at the outset into which of two categories the case falls:
(1) "direct discrimination", where the standard is discriminatory on
its face, or (2) "adverse effect discrimination", where the facially
neutral standard discriminates in effect:
Ontario Human Rights Commission
and O'Malley v. Simpsons-Sears Ltd.
,
1985 CanLII 18 (SCC)
, [1985] 2
S.C.R. 536 (hereinafter "
O'Malley
"), at p. 551,
per

McIntyre J. If a
prima facie
case of either form of discrimination is
established, the burden shifts to the employer to justify it.
[22]

[
43
]

After considering seven problems that arise when
applying the conventional approach to claims brought under human rights
legislation, she arrives at the following conclusion:

Whatever may have
once been the benefit of the conventional analysis of discrimination claims
brought under human rights legislation, the difficulties discussed show that
there is much to be said for now adopting a unified approach that (1) avoids
the problematic distinction between direct and adverse effect discrimination,
(2) requires employers to accommodate as much as reasonably possible the
characteristics of individual employees when setting the workplace standard,
and (3) takes a strict approach to exemptions from the duty not to
discriminate, while permitting exemptions where they are reasonably necessary
to the achievement of legitimate work-related objectives.
[23]

[
44
]

Having thus determined that a unified approach
to allegations of discrimination is needed, Justice McLachlin next sets out the
elements of such an approach:

Having considered
the various alternatives, I propose the following three-step test for
determining whether a
prima facie
discriminatory standard is a BFOR. An
employer may justify the impugned standard by establishing on the balance of
probabilities:

(1)

that the employer adopted the standard for a purpose rationally
connected to the performance of the job;

(2)

that the employer adopted the particular standard in an honest and
good faith belief that it was necessary to the fulfilment of that legitimate
work-related purpose; and

(3)

that the standard is reasonably necessary to the accomplishment of
that legitimate work-related purpose. To show that the standard is reasonably
necessary, it must be demonstrated that it is impossible to accommodate
individual employees sharing the characteristics of the claimant without
imposing undue hardship upon the employer.
[24]

[
45
]

Finally, Justice McLachlin describes her
proposed three-step test, making the following comments on its application:

The first step in
assessing whether the employer has successfully established a BFOR defence is
to identify the general purpose of the impugned standard and determine whether
it is rationally connected to the performance of the job. The initial task is
to determine what the impugned standard is generally designed to achieve.
[25]

[
46
]

Still
on the subject of this
first step, she affirms:

The employer must demonstrate that
there is a rational connection between the general purpose for which the
impugned standard was introduced and the objective requirements of the job.
[26]

[
47
]

She also specifies the following regarding step
one:

The focus at the
first step is not on the validity of the particular standard that is at issue,
but rather on the validity of its more general purpose. This inquiry is
necessarily more general than determining whether there is a rational
connection between the performance of the job and the
particular standard

that has been selected, as may have been the case on the conventional approach
.
[27]

[
48
]

Justice McLachlin then turns to step two:

Once the legitimacy
of the employer's more general purpose is established, the employer must take
the second step of demonstrating that it adopted the particular standard with
an honest and good faith belief that it was necessary to the accomplishment of
its purpose, with no intention of discriminating against the claimant. This
addresses the subjective element of the test which, although not essential to a
finding that the standard is not a BFOR, is one basis on which the standard may
be struck down: see
O'Malley, supra
, at pp. 547-50,
per
McIntyre
J.;
Etobicoke, supra
, at p. 209,
per
McIntyre J. If the
imposition of the standard was not thought to be reasonably necessary or was
motivated by discriminatory
animus
, then it cannot be a BFOR.

It is important to note that the
analysis shifts at this stage from the general purpose of the standard to the
particular standard itself.
[28]

[
49
]

Finally, Justice McLachlin elaborates on step
three:

The employer's third
and final hurdle is to demonstrate that the impugned standard is reasonably
necessary for the employer to accomplish its purpose, which by this point has
been demonstrated to be rationally connected to the performance of the job. The
employer must establish that it cannot accommodate the claimant and others
adversely affected by the standard without experiencing undue hardship. When
referring to the concept of "undue hardship", it is important to
recall the words of Sopinka J. who observed in
Central Okanagan School
District No. 23 v. Renaud
,
1992 CanLII 81 (S.C.C.)
, [1992] 2 S.C.R.
970, at p. 984, that "[t]he use of the term `undue' infers that some
hardship is acceptable; it is only `undue' hardship that satisfies this
test". It may be ideal from the employer's perspective to choose a
standard that is uncompromisingly stringent. Yet the standard, if it is to be
justified under the human rights legislation, must accommodate factors relating
to the unique capabilities and inherent worth and dignity of every individual,
up to the point of undue hardship.

When determining whether an
existing standard is reasonably necessary for the employer to accomplish its
purpose, it may be helpful to refer to the jurisprudence of this Court dealing
both with the justification of direct discrimination and the concept of
accommodation within the adverse effect discrimination analysis. For example,
dealing with adverse effect discrimination in
Central Alberta Dairy Pool
,
supra
, at pp. 520-21, Wilson J. addressed the factors that may be
considered when assessing an employer's duty to accommodate an employee to the
point of undue hardship. Among the relevant factors are the financial cost of
the possible method of accommodation, the relative interchangeability of the
workforce and facilities, and the prospect of substantial interference with the
rights of other employees. See also
Renaud
, supra
, at p. 984,
per

Sopinka J. The various factors are not entrenched, except to the extent that
they are expressly included or excluded by statute. In all cases, as Cory J.
noted in
Chambly, supra
, at p. 546, such considerations "should be
applied with common sense and flexibility in the context of the factual
situation presented in each case".
[29]

[
50
]

This concludes what in my view are the relevant
excerpts from
British Columbia (Public Service Employee Relations
Commission) v. BCGSEU
. I believe it is appropriate to point out that on
December 19, 1999, the Supreme Court of Canada reiterated the principles set
out in this judgment in
British Columbia (Superintendent of Motor Vehicles)
v. British Columbia (Council of Human Rights)
.
[30]

[
51
]

In the headnote of that judgment, which allowed
the appeal, the problem before the Court is described in the following terms:

The claimant suffered from a
condition called homonymous hemianopia (H.H.) which eliminated most of his
left-side peripheral vision in both eyes. The B.C. Superintendent of Motor
Vehicles cancelled his driver's licence on the ground that his vision no longer
met the standard of a minimum field of vision of 120 degrees. While exceptions
to this standard were permitted in other cases, people with H.H. are not
permitted to hold a driver's licence in B.C. After repeatedly being denied a
licence despite passing the requisite tests, the claimant filed a complaint
with the B.C. Council of Human Rights. The Council found that the standard was
prima
facie
direct discrimination and that the Superintendent had failed to show
that applying the visual field standards inflexibly, without individual
assessments, was reasonably necessary. The Superintendent was ordered to assess
the claimant and to place restrictions on his licence if necessary. A judge of
the Supreme Court of British Columbia dismissed the Superintendent's petition
for judicial review but the Court of Appeal set aside that decision. Since the
Court of Appeal's judgment, this Court has set out a modified test for
discrimination under the B.C.
Human Rights Code
-- the
Meiorin

test.
[31]

[
52
]

It is helpful to cite some of the findings of
the Court before it arrived at its final decision:

In summary, the
Superintendent offered no evidence that he had considered any of the options
that might have made an assessment of Mr. Grismer's driving abilities viable
and affordable. Content to rely on the general opinion of the medical
community, and ignoring the evidence that some people with H.H. can and do
drive safely, he offered not so much as a gesture in the direction of
accommodation. His position, quite simply, was that no accommodation was
necessary. Under the
Meiorin
test, it was incumbent on the Superintendent
to show that he had considered and reasonably rejected all viable forms of
accommodation. The onus was on the Superintendent, having adopted a
prima
facie
discriminatory standard, to prove that incorporating aspects of
individual accommodation within the standard was impossible short of undue
hardship. The Superintendent did not do so. On the facts of this case, the
Superintendent's blanket refusal to issue a driver's licence was not justified.
He fell into error in this case not because he refused to lower his safety
standards (which would be contrary to the public interest), but because he
abandoned his reasonable approach to licensing and adopted an absolute standard
which was not supported by convincing evidence. The Superintendent was obliged
to give Mr. Grismer the opportunity to prove whether or not he could drive
safely, by assessing Mr. Grismer individually. It follows that the charge of
discrimination under the
Human Rights Act
was established.

This is the
conclusion that the
Meiorin
test requires, on the evidence and findings
in this case. The question may be put, however, whether this approach places
too high an evidentiary burden on the government, particularly in situations
involving public safety. The obvious answer to this question is that it is the
Legislature, not the Court, which has placed the evidentiary burden of showing
reasonable necessity once
prima facie
discrimination has been made out.
More fundamentally, is it really inappropriate to require a governmental body
that rejects an application for a driver's licence on the basis of disability
to prove on a balance of probabilities that the denial is reasonably necessary
to the standard of highway safety it has selected? The government authority
knows why it makes the denial and is in the best position to defend it. The
government must only establish its justification according to the relaxed
standard of proof on a balance of probabilities. Common sense and intuitive
reasoning are not excluded, but in a case where accommodation is flatly refused
there must be some evidence to link the outright refusal of even the
possibility of accommodation with an undue safety risk. If the government
agency can show that accommodation is impossible without risking safety or that
it imposes some other form of undue hardship, then it can maintain the absolute
prohibition. If not, it is under an obligation to accommodate the claimant by
allowing the person an opportunity to show that he or she does not present an
undue threat to safety.

This case deals with
no more than the right to be accommodated. It does not decide that Mr. Grismer
had the right to a driver's licence. It merely establishes that he had a
right
to be assessed
. That was all the Member found and all that we assert. The
discrimination here lies not in the refusal to give Mr. Grismer a driver's
licence, but in the refusal to even permit him to attempt to demonstrate that
his situation could be accommodated without jeopardizing the Superintendent's
goal of reasonable road safety. This decision stands for the proposition that
those who provide services subject to the
Human Rights Code
must adopt
standards that accommodate people with disabilities where this can be done
without sacrificing their legitimate objectives and without incurring undue
hardship. It does not suggest that agencies like the Motor Vehicle Branch must
lower their safety standards or engage in accommodation efforts that amount to
undue hardship.

Nor should this
decision be taken as predetermining the result in other cases. This appeal is
essentially a judicial review of a decision of a human rights tribunal in a
particular case. The result flows from the evidence called before and accepted
by the Member in this case. The Member found that the Superintendent had not met
the burden of proving that a blanket refusal without the possibility of
individual accommodation was reasonably necessary under the Act. In another
case, on other evidence, that burden might be met.
[32]

[
53
]

We must now attempt to apply the principles as
set out by the Supreme Court of Canada in the two cases cited above to the
matter presently before this Court. Obviously, these principles must be read in
the context of the present matter, which differs from that of the two Supreme
Court cases. In particular, it should be emphasized that the present case
involves a private relationship between a syndicate of co-owners and certain
individual co-owners, while the two Supreme Court cases involved the
relationship between individuals and State authorities.

[
54
]

Applying the three-step approach set out in
British
Columbia (Public Service Employee Relations Commission) v. BCGSEU
first
requires posing the following question: can the respondent, that is, the
syndicate of Place Northcrest co-owners, justify the restrictions set out in
the declaration of co-ownership by establishing on a balance of probabilities
that the restrictions imposed are rationally connected to the administration of
the immovable?

[
55
]

Before formulating an answer, it is important
once again to recall Justice McLachlin's statement regarding this question:

The focus at the first step is not
on the validity of the particular standard that is at issue, but rather on the
validity of its more general purpose.

[
56
]

Relying on this statement, I have no hesitation
in answering the first question in the affirmative, in light of
article 1039
of
the
Civil Code of Québec
,
which reads as follows:

1039. Upon the publication of the
declaration of co-ownership, the co-owners as a body constitute a legal person,
the objects of which are to preserve the immovable, to maintain and manage the
common portions, to protect the rights appurtenant to the immovable or the
co-ownership and to take all measures of common interest.

The legal person is called a
syndicate.

[
57
]

It seems clear that the purpose of the impugned
standards is precisely "
to preserve the
immovable, to maintain and manage the common portions, to protect the rights
appurtenant to the immovable or the co-ownership and to take all measures of
common interest
".

[
58
]

Having answered the first question in the
affirmative, I now turn my attention to the second: has the syndicate of
co-owners established that the standards set out in clauses 2.6.3, 6.5, 6.16
and 9.3 of the declaration of co-ownership were adopted in good faith and with
an honest belief that they were necessary to accomplish the legitimate purpose
noted in the preceding paragraph, with no intention of discriminating against
the appellants?

[
59
]

Again, I must answer in the affirmative, this
time relying on
article 1056
of the
Civil Code of Québec
, cited above.
In fact, I have already answered this question in these reasons, seeing as it
is the second of the six questions formulated by the trial judge and set out at
the beginning of his decision. It is neither useful nor necessary to elaborate
further on this subject.

[
60
]

The application of
British Columbia (Public
Service Employees Relations Commission) v. BCGSEU
thus compels us to ask a
third question: has the syndicate of co-owners established that the standards
the appellants are challenging were necessary to accomplish its legitimate
purpose by showing that it was impossible to accommodate the appellants or
other persons who share their beliefs without experiencing undue hardship?

[
61
]

In answering this question, it is useful to
recall once again Justice McLachlin's comment on the third step of her proposed
test:

When determining whether an
existing standard is reasonably necessary for the employer to accomplish its
purpose, it may be helpful to refer to the jurisprudence of this Court dealing
both with the justification of direct discrimination and the concept of
accommodation within the adverse effect discrimination analysis.
[33]

[
62
]

Accordingly, this is precisely what the trial
judge did as he sought an answer to the fourth question raised at the beginning
of his judgment. After a lengthy analysis of the duty to accommodate, he
finally concluded the following:

[
translation
]

On the whole, the Court is of the
view that the syndicate fulfilled its duty to accommodate, thereby
re-establishing equality between the different co-owners.
[34]

[
63
]

The appellants contest this conclusion, relying
on the same type of arguments as those raised to counter the response of the
trial judge to the second question. In other words, they invite this Court to
substitute its own assessment of the evidence for that of the trial judge and
to conclude that the respondent did not fulfill its duty to accommodate the
appellants.

[
64
]

In my view, the trial judge made no serious
error that would justify the intervention of this Court. On the contrary, it
was the intransigent attitude adopted by the appellants who systematically
refused every proposal that did not correspond precisely to their demands that
made accommodation practically impossible.

[
65
]

It should be noted here that, contrary to what
was argued by the appellants, the respondent's refusal to submit to their
demands was not motivated by stubbornness but by the desire to avoid the very
situation the restrictions in the declaration of co-ownership sought to
forestall. Specifically, they wished to prevent any marring or loss of value of
the two buildings constituting Place Northcrest caused by mismatched objects on
the balconies and terraces or in the immediate surroundings of the buildings.

[
66
]

This concern goes beyond the theoretical and targets
more than just the construction of succahs. This is clear in the following
excerpts from a letter from Micheline Larochelle, the syndicate manager, to the
residents of Place Northcrest, dated January 28, 1992 (exhibit R-12):

[
translation
]

In recent months, a number of
owners have brought to our attention flags, sheds (Succot) and Christmas
decorations (lights) on the balconies and terraces. Furthermore, last summer
some occupants placed flower-boxes or stored folding chairs in the passageways.
The balconies and terraces are limited common portions and may not be used like
the exclusive portions (dwelling units) for personal reasons.

No one may put up a sign displaying
their political, religious or national allegiance, nor any other sign
containing information regarding profession, sale or rental, etc. The building
would quickly take on the appearance of an international fair or an enormous
billboard.

[
67
]

Indeed, the syndicate had to deal with a number
of complaints about failures to comply with the restrictions set out in the
declaration of co-ownership. The trial judge found that the syndicate dealt
with these complaints fairly, striving to maintain a balance between the
individual rights of the co-owners and the collective rights of the group to
which they belong. In the present case, however, this balance could not be
achieved because of the inflexible attitudes of the appellants who, as the
trial judge pointed out, [
translation
]
"
demonstrated neither tractability nor the will
to compromise
", contrary to what is required according to Justice
McIntyre in
Ontario Human Rights Commission
v. Simpsons-Sears
:

The employer must
take reasonable steps towards that end which may or may not result in full
accommodation. Where such reasonable steps, however, do not fully reach the
desired end, the complainant, in the absence of some accommodating steps on his
own part such as an acceptance in this case of part-time work, must either
sacrifice his religious principles or his employment.
[35]

[
68
]

It is relevant to cite the trial judge's
description of the behaviour of the respective parties in the present case:

[
translation
]

The undisputed evidence shows that
the syndicate had a respectful attitude toward the rights of the respondents.
The administrators and members designated by the board of directors met with
the respondents on several occasions. The syndicate gave the respondents the
opportunity to share their point of view at a general meeting. As soon as the
syndicate became aware of the respondents' serious objection to the
restrictions on the balconies, it increased its efforts to find reasonable
accommodation.

The arrangement it proposed
consisted of erecting a common succah at an acceptable location on the land
adjacent to the building, which would make it possible for the respondents to
comply with the religious precept. The syndicate made every effort to find a
solution to all of the problems the respondents brought up; for example, they
dealt with supplying electricity to certain doors, turning off a security
system, and linking the existing building with the succah to be built a few
metres away from the building. These technical adjustments were necessary to
meet the requirements of Jewish religious law. The cost of building the succah
would be borne by the co-owners as a whole.

As soon as the syndicate solved one
of the technical problems, the respondents raised another, and they continued
to look for problems during the hearing. It has been demonstrated that, on a
balance of probabilities, it is possible to build a succah at the planned
location with the necessary modifications to the building's alarm and
electrical systems to permit the respondents to go there in compliance with the
applicable religious precepts.
[36]

[
69
]

It is apparent from these observations that the
solutions presented by the respondent in its effort to accommodate were
consistently turned down point blank by the appellants. Basing myself on the
above-cited comments of Justice McIntyre, I believe the appellants will have to
sacrifice their right to live in Place Northcrest if they are unable to comply
with the restrictions set out in the co-ownership agreement they freely signed.

[
70
]

As I have already pointed out, the situation of
the parties in the present case is not the same as those of the parties in
British
Columbia (Public Service Employees Relations Commission) v. BCGSEU
and
British
Columbia (Superintendent of Motor Vehicles) v. British Columbia (Council of
Human Rights)
.
In the first, a woman was deprived of her employment, while
in the second, a man was refused the right to drive a motor vehicle; neither of
these individuals had been presented with alternatives. In the present case,
however, the appellants could easily choose to live someplace other than Place
Northcrest if they refuse to make any concessions whatsoever in terms of the
practice of their religious beliefs.

[
71
]

In both of the cases mentioned above, the
Supreme Court affirmed that the duty to accommodate must be appreciated in
light of the particular circumstances of each case. Applying this rule, I find
that the respondent has fulfilled its duty to accommodate by making reasonable
offers to the appellants and that it would experience undue hardship if it were
required to meet the appellants' demands.

[
72
]

On the whole, I find that the third branch of
the test set out by Justice McLachlin in
British Columbia (Public Service
Employees Relations Commission) v. BCGSEU
must be responded to in the
affirmative. This in turn leads me to conclude that the trial judge was correct
in arriving at an affirmative answer to the fourth question he set out at the
beginning of his judgment.

[
73
]

The trial judge could have stopped there and
concluded that the restrictions imposed in the declaration of co-ownership were
justified despite their impact on the appellants' freedom of religion. On the
contrary, however, he chose to continue his analysis and address the question
of whether the restrictions were justified under
section 9.1
of the
Charter
of human rights and freedoms
, cited above.
[37]

[
74
]

In his analysis, the trial judge found that
building succahs on balconies or terraces could cause a security risk for the
residents and affect the rights of the other co-owners to enjoy their property
according to the terms of their agreement. He subsequently examined the
interaction between the fundamental rights set out in
sections 1
,
3
, and
6
of
the
Charter of human rights and freedoms
. Section 3 is cited above.
Sections 1 and 6 read as follows:

1. Every human being has a right to
life, and to personal security, inviolability and freedom.

6. Every
person has a right to the peaceful enjoyment and free disposition of his
property, except to the extent provided by law.

[
75
]

An examination of the provisions in light of

section 9.1
led him to the following conclusion:

[
translation
]

Fundamental rights are not arranged
in hierarchical order. One fundamental right does not yield in favour of
another one. Instead, there must be an attempt to enforce the different
fundamental rights in a harmonious manner. The rights of the co-owners as a
group to enjoy their property according to their established and consensual
agreements are, from the perspective of the
Charter of human rights and
freedoms
, as important as all the other fundamental freedoms set out in the
same
Charter
. It is truly accommodation that makes it possible for the
two rights to co-exist.
[38]

[
76
]

Although I am not prepared to make as bold a
statement as that contained in the first sentence of the above-cited paragraph,
I do agree with the notion that the different fundamental rights must be applied
in a manner that avoids privileging one over another, to the degree that this
is possible. This is where the notion of accommodation comes into play,
representing in this sense an attempt to harmonize the enforcement of the
various rights, undertaken in the spirit embodied in
section 9.1
of
the

Charter of human rights and freedoms
.

[
77
]

At this point in his analysis, although he did
not expressly acknowledge it, the trial judge found himself assessing the
impact of
section 10
of the
Charter
. Section 10 reads as follows:

10. Every person has a right to
full and equal recognition and exercise of his human rights and freedoms,
without distinction, exclusion or preference based on race, colour, sex,
pregnancy, sexual orientation, civil status, age except as provided by law,
religion, political convictions, language, ethnic or national origin, social
condition, a handicap or the use of any means to palliate a handicap.

Discrimination exists where such a
distinction, exclusion or preference has the effect of nullifying or impairing
such right.

[
78
]

The trial judge dealt with section 10 while
reflecting on whether there was reason to consider the possibility of a
justification under
section 9.1
of the
Charter

for the infringement on
freedom of religion. He answered this question in the following terms, citing a
decision of the Supreme Court of Canada:

[
translation
]

In
Devine v. Attorney General of
Quebec
, the Supreme Court stated the following on the interaction between
rights and freedoms (
sections 1
to 8), the test for justification under
section
9.1
, and equality rights in
section 10
of the
Charter
:

While it is true that
s. 9.1
does not apply to the principle of
equality enshrined in s. 10, it does apply to the guarantee of free expression
enshrined in
s. 3
. Whenever it is alleged that a distinction on a ground
prohibited by s. 10 has the effect of impairing or nullifying a right under s.
3, the scope of
s. 3
must still be determined in light of
s. 9.1
. Where, as
here,
s. 9.1
operates to limit the scope of freedom of expression guaranteed
under
s. 3
, s. 10 cannot be invoked to circumvent those reasonable limits and
to substitute an absolute guarantee of free expression. On the other hand,
having specified the scope of free expression,
s. 9.1
cannot be invoked to
justify a limit upon equal recognition and exercise of the right guaranteed by

s. 3
.
[39]

[
79
]

The trial judge determined that freedom of
religion, like freedom of expression, does not benefit from an absolute and
limitless guarantee. He subsequently arrived at the following conclusion:

[
translation
]

For these reasons, the Court is of
the view that the purpose sought through the terms of the declaration of
co-ownership are legitimate. The measures were enforced reasonably and were
rationally connected to their purpose. Without repeating the analysis of the
issue of reasonable accommodation, it is the opinion of the Court, for the
reasons set out above, that the restrictions imposed on the co-owners
constitute reasonable limits, particularly as they apply to portions subject to
a common property right.
[40]

[
80
]

In my view, in reaching the above conclusion,
the trial judge correctly responded to the fifth question he had set out at the
beginning of his judgment.

[
81
]

Furthermore, I am also of the opinion that the
judge implicitly answered another question, which can be stated as follows: are
sections 2.6.3, 6.5, 6.16 and 9.3 of the declaration of co-ownership null
pursuant to sections 10 and 13 of the
Charter of human rights and liberties
?

[
82
]

Section 10 is cited above. Section 13 reads as
follows:

13. No one may in a juridical act
stipulate a clause involving discrimination.

Such a clause is without effect.

[
83
]

It seems clear that the answers to the fourth
and fifth questions inevitably lead to a negative response to the question
raised above. Indeed, once it is clear that freedom of religion is not absolute
and cannot be invoked without considering the rights of others, it is no longer
possible to maintain that the clause in a contract stipulating an acceptable
limit to this freedom must be considered discriminatory under
sections 10
and

13
of the
Charter
.

[
84
]

This is the conclusion that emerges upon the
application of the excerpt from
Devine v. Attorney General of Quebec,
which
is cited by the trial judge and which I rely upon in these reasons.

[
85
]

I must point out that the trial judge himself
came to this conclusion, although he did so while answering his third question
and relying on the restrictive notion of freedom of religion that he had
adopted. In so doing, he arrived at the correct destination, but he took a
prohibited shortcut.

The right to injunction

[
86
]

Finally, the sixth question raised by the trial
judge, which deals with the application of
article 1080
of the
Civil Code of
Québec
, remains to be addressed. This article reads as follows:

1080. Where the refusal of a
co-owner to comply with the declaration of co-ownership causes serious and
irreparable prejudice to the syndicate or to one of the co-owners, either of
them may apply to the court for an injunction ordering the co-owner to comply with
the declaration.

If the co-owner violates the
injunction or refuses to obey it, the court may, in addition to the other
penalties it may impose, order the sale of the co-owner’s fraction, in
accordance with the provisions of the
Code of Civil Procedure
regarding
the sale of the property of others.

[
87
]

The trial judge, who responded to the sixth
question affirmatively, correctly interpreted this provision. The article,
which must be read as a whole, authorizes the court to order the sale of a
fraction of a building in divided co-ownership when the owner of this fraction
causes serious and irreparable prejudice to the syndicate or to one of the
co-owners by refusing to comply with the declaration of co-ownership and by
violating an injunction ordering him to comply. This article does not have the
effect of preventing the syndicate or the co-owners from applying for an
injunction in circumstances other than those just described. It merely adds the
possibility of a stronger sanction, that is, the sale of a fraction, when the
conditions mentioned in the article exist.

[
88
]

The trial judge therefore did not err in issuing
a permanent injunction after stating the following on the applicable rule:

[
translation
]

In the civil law, specific
performance is the rule. Execution by equivalence [
translation
] "is considered a secondary form of
performance, which the creditor is not obliged to accept."
[41]

[
89
]

For these reasons, I would dismiss the appeal,
with costs.

[
