]

When purchasing an apartment in a building held
in divided co-ownership, the new co-owner agrees to respect the obligations and
restrictions set out in the declaration of co-ownership. If some of the clauses
of the declaration have the effect of preventing the practice of religious
rites on the balconies, porches and patios adjacent to the co-owner's apartment
and reserved for the exclusive use of the co-owner, can a court refuse to
enforce these clauses? This is the question to be decided in the present
matter, which revolves essentially around the application of the
Charter of
human rights and freedoms
(S.R.Q. c. C-12) (
Charter
) to contractual
matters between private parties.

THE FACTS

[
91
]

The appellants, who describe themselves as
practising orthodox Jews, are co-owners of apartments in two high-rises of
Place Northcrest in Montreal, also known as phases VI and VII of the Sanctuaire
du Mont-Royal. The two buildings are in divided co-ownership and are
administered by the respondent, the Syndicat Northcrest.

[
92
]

In the fall of 1997, the appellant Amselem
requested permission from the syndicate to erect a succah to celebrate the
Jewish festival of Succot. Because this was prohibited in the declaration of
co-ownership, the syndicate refused, although it did offer to construct a large
tent near one of the apartment buildings that could be used as a common succah
by all the Jewish co-owners who wished to celebrate Succot.

[
93
]

The appellants, who viewed this offer as
unacceptable despite the approval of the Canadian Jewish Congress, Quebec
region, proceeded to set up succahs on their respective balconies, porches, and
patios.

[
94
]

In response, the syndicate undertook injunction
proceedings, which gave rise to the judgment now being appealed.

JUDGMENT AT FIRST INSTANCE

[
95
]

The trial judge organized his judgment around
the following six questions:

[
translation
]

1.

What are the restrictions set out in the
co-ownership agreement?

2.

Are these restrictions justified by the
destination, characteristics or location of the immovable?

3.

Do these restrictions infringe on the freedom of
religion and equality rights of the respondents?

4.

If so, did the respondent offer reasonable
accommodation to correct this inequality?

5.

If so, is the infringement justified under

section 9.1
of the
Charter
?

6.

In the absence of serious and irreparable
prejudice, may a co-owner be compelled to comply with the declaration of
co-ownership (art. 1080 C.C.Q.)?

[
96
]

After analyzing the declaration of co-ownership
signed by the appellants, the trial judge answered the first question by
affirming that clauses 2.6.3., 6.5, 6.16 and 9.3 of the declaration prohibited
all owners from enclosing their balconies, porches and patios, from installing
on them any type of construction whatsoever, from making any alteration to
them, and from placing any decoration or anything at all on them with the
exception of usual outdoor furniture. After noting that these restrictions
existed to ensure the preservation of the uniform exterior appearance of the
immovable, the trial judge pointed out that the act constituting co-ownership
i) defined the destination of the immovable as exclusively residential, ii)
specified that it was an upscale complex, and iii) placed a particular
importance on the exterior harmony of the immovable. As for the second
question, he answered that the restrictions imposed on the co-owners regarding
the use of balconies, porches and patios were in compliance with the principles
set out in article 1056 C.C.Q.

[
97
]

In passing, he noted that the evidence showed
that the respondent had applied the restrictions set out in the declaration in
a consistent and uniform manner ever since it had become responsible for the
administration of the immovable in 1991.

[
98
]

Proceeding to his third question, the trial
judge examined the effect of the restrictions on the appellants. Recognizing
that discrimination may be indirect and take the form of adverse effects on one
or several persons, his analysis does not focus on whether or not distinctions
directly targeting the appellants exist, but rather on what constitutes an
infringement of freedom of religion. In his opinion, [
translation
] "
in order to
enforce their equality rights and their right to freedom of religion and
thereby invalidate a contractual clause
," the appellants [
translation
] "
must first establish that the restrictions in the act of
co-ownership have infringed on their freedom of religion
".

[
99
]

After a review of the case law, he determined
that freedom of religion can be relied on only if there is a connection between
the right asserted and what is considered mandatory pursuant to the religious
teaching upon which the right is based. In his view, the evidence showed that
the Jewish religion did not oblige practising Jews to possess their own succahs
and that there was no commandment prescribing where they must be erected. He
concluded that the application of the restrictions agreed upon in the declaration
of co-ownership did not infringe on freedom of religion.

[
100
]

In the event that this conclusion were set aside, the trial judge
added that the respondent was respectful of the appellants' rights, gave them
the opportunity to present their point of view, and proposed reasonable
accommodation by offering to build, at the cost of the co-owners as a group, a
common succah on the land adjacent to the building at a location that would
make it possible for them to comply with their religion. He criticized the
appellants for the lack of flexibility they demonstrated by refusing the
suggested compromise. In his view, their attitude showed that they did not wish
to participate in finding a mutually acceptable solution.

[
101
]

Addressing the fifth question, he noted that the act constituting
the co-ownership created a right of way on the balconies to be used in
emergency situations and to ensure the safety of individuals. In his view, this
right to security is also a fundamental right and, seeing as the
Charter

does not create a hierarchy of rights, it therefore merits consideration equal
to that accorded freedom of religion.

[
102
]

The judge then turned to the question of whether the restrictions
could be justified. Basing himself on
R. v. Oakes
,
[42]
he developed a justification test for
contractual matters and ultimately found that the purposes of the restrictions
in the declaration of co-ownership were legitimate and that the manner in which
they were adopted was reasonable and rational with respect to the objective
sought. He concluded that the restrictions imposed on the co-owners were
reasonable limits within the meaning of
section 9.1
of the
Charter
,
particularly since they dealt with the common portions of the co-owned
property.

[
103
]

Finally, the trial judge turned to the sixth question, which called
for the interpretation of article 1080 C.C.Q. Affirming that [
translation
] "
it is far from apparent that the installation of succahs
fifteen days a year would cause serious prejudice for the syndicate and/or the
other co-owners
" and that the notion of "
serious and irreparable prejudice
" as required
by this article must be adapted, he subsequently concluded that
article 1080

C.C.Q. does not prevent specific performance from being obtained by injunction.
Rather, he determined, the provision merely adds an additional sanction by
authorizing the sale of the co-owner's fraction if the latter refuses to comply
with such an order.

[
104
]

For these reasons, the trial judge issued a permanent injunction
ordering the appellants to refrain from erecting any shelter, structure,
construction or succah whatsoever on common portions reserved for exclusive use
of the co-ownership. He also authorized the syndicate to proceed with their
demolition, if applicable.

SUBMISSIONS OF THE PARTIES

[
105
]

First, the appellants maintain that nothing in the declaration of
co-ownership prohibits the setting up of succahs on their balconies and that
the syndicate should have authorized them to do so.

[
106
]

Alternatively, they submit that, pursuant to
sections 3
and
10
of
the
Charter
, they have the right to exercise their freedom of religion
by practising what they consider to be a mandatory rite, namely, the
performance of certain activities in a succah during a specific time of the
year. At page 37 of their factum, they state:

We submit that not only
Article 10

of the
Charter
applies, in the manner approached by the trial judge, but
also that
Article 3
applies on its own, separately and independently from
Article 10. The difference has theoretical and practical implications. For
instance, not all the liberties protected under
Article 3
are listed as grounds
which may not be discriminated against in Article 10. In our case, the
importance lies in the rule about the "reasonable accommodation"
discussed by the trial judge vis-à-vis the "reasonable limits"
provision of
Article 9.1
of the
Charter
(which is comparable to
Article
1
of the
Canadian
Charter of Rights and Freedoms
) which was not
discussed. Certainly any resident of Quebec may invoke both
Articles 3
and 10
of the
Charter
, and this is what we do here.

[
107
]

Finally, they submit that
article 1080
C.C.Q. has the effect of
restricting the remedy of injunction in matters of co-ownership to cases where
the syndicate has established serious or irreparable prejudice,
[43]
and that the erection of a succah on a
balcony for 8 to 10 days each year does not meet this threshold.

[
108
]

For its part, the League for Human Rights of B'nai Brith Canada,
intervener at first instance and appellant before this Court, supports the
position of the appellants, but focuses on the content of freedom of religion,
submitting that the trial judge overstepped his jurisdiction by deciding what
the commandments of the Jewish religion were instead of relying on the sincere
beliefs of the appellants.

[
109
]

The respondent answers by arguing that the declaration of
co-ownership prohibits what it considers the construction of succahs on patios
and balconies, common portions reserved for exclusive use, and that this
prohibition is justified by the destination of the immovable. It adds that succahs
on the balconies, patios and porches would compromise safety and be considered
an increased risk that could cause its insurance to be suspended.

[
110
]

It also maintains that the restrictions in the declaration of
co-ownership are in no way discriminatory since they treat all religions
equally and that the trial judge did not err in his definition of freedom of
religion or in concluding that the syndicate had offered appropriate
accommodation, in the event that there was in fact discrimination, which it denies.

ANALYSIS

I.

Scope of the restrictions

[
111
]

The declaration of co-ownership contains the following clauses:

2.6.3.
Balconies, porches and
patios

The owner of each exclusive
portion (dwelling unit) with a door leading to a balcony, porch or patio
adjoining his or her exclusive portion (dwelling unit) has the personal and
exclusive use of the balcony, or of the portion of the porch adjoining his or
her exclusive potion
, subject to the following
rules:

a)

on porches, an area at least as wide as is
required under fire safety by-laws must be kept free of garden furniture and
other accessories, as the porches serve as emergency exits.

b)

No owner may enclose or block off any
balcony, porch or patio in any manner whatsoever or erect thereon constructions
of any kind whatsoever.

c)

Balconies constructed as terraces or patios are
reserved for the private and exclusive use of the owner of each exclusive
portion (dwelling unit) with a door leading to the aforesaid balcony or patio,
but the maintenance of these terraces or patios (including the mowing of lawns)
is a common duty.

…

6.5 Uniformity of décor in the
building

Entrance doors to the exclusive
portions (dwelling units), windows, painted exterior surfaces and,
in
general, any exterior elements contributing to the overall harmony of the
building's appearance may under no circumstances be altered, even if they are
part of the limited common portions
, without first obtaining the written
permission of the Board of Directors, who themselves must first obtain the
approval of the co-owners at a general meeting.

6.16 Exterior decorations
prohibited

Co-owners may not decorate, paint
or alter the exterior of the exclusive portions in any way whatsoever without
first obtaining the written consent of the Board of Directors, subject to any
exception provided for in this declaration.

9.3 Balconies and porches

Subject to the law and to this
declaration, each co-owner having exclusive use of a balcony or a potion of a
porch adjoining his or her exclusive portion (dwelling unit), as provided for
in clause 2.6.3, shall keep said balcony or portion of the porch clean. The
co-owner having exclusive use of said balcony or portion of the porch is solely
responsible for the day-to-day maintenance thereof. However, the Board of
Directors is responsible for the replacement of or repairs to said balconies
and porches as a common expense, unless the balcony or porch must be repaired
or replaced because of the fault or negligence of a co-owner or someone for
whom that co-owner is legally responsible, in which case the costs and expense
of any repairs or replacement shall be assumed by the co-owner in question.

Furthermore, subject to acts and
regulations of general application,
nothing other than usual outdoor
furniture may be left or stored on a balcony or porch
without first
obtaining permission in writing from the Board of Directors. Under no
circumstances may balconies or porches be used for drying laundry, towels, etc.

No balcony or porch may be
decorated, covered, enclosed or painted in any way whatsoever without the prior
written permission of the co-owners or the Board of Directors, as the case may
be.

(Emphasis added)

[
112
]

As the trial judge determined, the impugned clauses of the act of
co-ownership prohibit,
inter alia
, the installation of succahs on balconies,
porches and patios, which are common portions pursuant to the act of
co-ownership. Because these portions are conceived as natural extensions of the
adjoining apartments, however, the respective owners of the apartments are
awarded exclusive use in the declaration.

[
113
]

These clauses therefore limit the uses to which owners of the
adjoining apartments may put these balconies, porches or patios. In this sense,
they restrict the rights of the co-owners.

II.

Validity of restrictions under the
Civil Code

[
114
]

Article 1056 C.C.Q. places limits on restrictions on the rights of
co-owners in the following terms:

No declaration of co-ownership may
impose any restriction on the rights of the co-owners except restrictions
justified by the destination, characteristics or location of the immovable.

[
115
]

As this Court stated in
Kilzi v. Syndicat des copropriétaires du
104000 boul.
L'Acadie
,
[44]
the
validity of the restrictions under the
Civil Code
is determined by
referring to all the contractual clauses as a whole, the physical characteristics
and location of the immovable, and the social circumstances of the occupants.

[
116
]

In the present case, the evidence establishes that the impugned
clauses were adopted essentially to preserve the style and external appearance
of the immovable as an upscale residential building and, alternatively, for
security reasons (evacuation of the building in certain exceptional
circumstances). In my view, this is sufficient to render them valid within the
meaning of
article 1056
C.C.Q., and I share the conclusions of my colleague
Morin and the trial judge on this point.

III.

Validity of restrictions under the

Charter

[
117
]

If the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms

applies only
to state action, the
Quebec
Charter of human rights and liberties
, for
its part, establishes a double rights-protection regime, [
translation
] "
since it aims, on the one hand, to sanction private
infringements on specific rights and freedoms while, on the other hand,
checking state action that could violate these same rights and freedoms
."
[45]

[
118
]

In the present case, the appellants submit that the impugned clauses
prohibit them from exercising their religious beliefs by installing a succah on
their balconies, porches or patios and are consequently invalid according to

section 3
of the
Charter
,
[46]
which
reads as follows:

Every person is the possessor of
the fundamental freedoms, including freedom of conscience, freedom of religion,
freedom of opinion, freedom of expression, freedom of peaceful assembly and
freedom of association.

[
119
]

In my view, they have incorrectly presented the problem. We should
not lose sight of the fact that the impugned clauses are not found in a
normative text adopted by the legislator, the government or any other power
upon which the law has conferred the authority to impose norms (
section 56(3)

of the
Charter
). If they were, the Court would be compelled to determine
whether they placed a restriction on the freedom of religion of the appellants
and if so, whether they were in compliance with
section 9.1
of the
Charter
.
Rather, these clauses are found in a contract the appellants freely entered
into upon purchasing their dwelling unit in co-ownership at Northcrest. With
great respect for the appellants, their factum and pleadings obscure this
crucial point.

[
120
]

Indeed, as the Supreme Court stated in
Frenette v. Métropolitan
Life Insurance Co.
,
[47]

granting a right or freedom quasi-constitutional protection by incorporating it
within the
Charter
does not make it an absolute right which may not be
waived through a contract.

[
121
]

In that case, our highest court concluded that the right to respect
for one's private life (
section 5
of the
Charter
) and the right to
professional secrecy (
section 9
of the
Charter
) were not absolute rights
that could be derogated from solely in exceptional circumstances and,
consequently, that the insured could waive the right at the time of the life
insurance application by signing a form authorizing the insurer to have access
to his medical records.

[
122
]

Nor is freedom of religion an absolute right, as the Supreme Court
recently pointed out in
Trinity Western University v. College of Teachers
.
[48]
Parties may therefore adjust or even
restrict this right through contractual agreement. The same is true for the
other fundamental freedoms set out in
section 3
of the
Charter
.

[
123
]

In addition, the restriction or waiver of a right protected by the
Charter
,
once validly accepted in a contract, may be set aside only through the
application of a provision in
Chapter I.1
of the
Charter
, "Right to
Equal Recognition and Exercise of Rights and Freedoms" (sections 10.1 to
20.1).

[
124
]

In the present case, because the question is not related to working
conditions, the only applicable
Charter
provision is section 13:

No one may in a juridical act
stipulate a clause involving discrimination.

Such a clause is without effect.

[
125
]

In this provision, the Parliament of Quebec has given precedence to
the right to freedom from discrimination over the will of the parties to a
contract. This appears to be in perfect agreement with the importance that is
to be conferred on the right to dignity, a fundamental concept underlying all
charters or human rights declarations, including the
Charter
, which is
explicit in its preamble:

Whereas all human beings are equal
in worth and dignity, and are entitled to equal protection of the law;

[
126
]

Discrimination infringes upon the right to the respect all persons
deserve as human beings. It is prohibited by
section 13
of the
Charter
,
which stipulates that any discriminatory clause is null despite the will of the
parties involved, even if this will is still valid because the party
discriminated against has not applied for the annulment of the contract. In
other words, a discriminatory contractual clause is contrary to public order.
[49]

[
127
]

In my view, it is undeniable that a declaration of co-ownership is a
juridical act within the terms of
section 13
of the
Charter
. We must
then consider whether the provisions therein regarding the use of balconies,
porches and patios are discriminatory.

[
128
]

What constitutes discrimination is defined in
section 10
of the
Charter

as follows:

Every person has a right to full
and equal recognition and exercise of his human rights and freedoms, without
distinction, exclusion or preference based on race, colour, sex, pregnancy,
sexual orientation, civil status, age except as provided by law, religion,
political convictions, language, ethnic or national origin, social condition, a
handicap or the use of any means to palliate a handicap.

Discrimination exists where such a
distinction, exclusion or preference has the effect of nullifying or impairing
such right.

[
129
]

Commenting on this section in light of the case law,
[50]
this Court wrote the following in a recent
judgment,
Quebec (A.G.) v. Lambert,

J.E. 2002-527 at para. 72
:

[
translation
]

Discrimination exists:

(a)

when there is a
distinction, exclusion or preference;

(b)

when this
distinction, exclusion or preference
is based on
one of the grounds enumerated in the first paragraph of
section 10
of the
Charter
;
and

(c)

when the
distinction, exclusion or preference
has the effect
of destroying or compromising the right to full equality in the recognition and
exercise of a human right or freedom.

[
130
]

Before analyzing the evidence in the present case according to these
three steps, I believe like the trial judge that it is useful to note that the
discrimination prohibited under the
Charter
may, as the case law makes
clear,
[51]
be
direct or by an adverse effect felt by one or several persons because of their
personal characteristics.

[
131
]

As Justice McLachlin noted in the Meiroin case,
[52]
where discrimination resulting from a
statute or standard adopted by a public authority is alleged, it is the
substantive effect of the impugned provision that must be examined. In my view,
the same is true when the alleged discrimination results from a contract.

[
132
]

In order to succeed, the appellants must establish that they are
prevented from full and equal enjoyment of a protected freedom on the basis of
a ground prohibited in
section 10
of the
Charter
.
[53]

Distinction, exclusion or preference

[
133
]

In order to establish distinction, exclusion or preference, we must
first determine whether the impugned clauses affect the appellants differently
than they do other persons. In short, we must define the groups.

[
134
]

Seeing as the restrictions are set out in a contract that binds only
the co-owners of the Northcrest, it is appropriate to compare the situation of
the appellants with that of the other co-owners in the two high-rises.

[
135
]

Clearly, the impugned clauses of the declaration of co-ownership
have the substantive effect of preventing the appellants from installing a
succah on their balcony, porch or patio. In this sense, are they affected
differently from the other co-owners?

[
136
]

At first glance, the impugned clauses are neutral and have the
effect of prohibiting
all
co-owners from installing any object other
than the usual furniture on their balconies, porches or patios.

[
137
]

The appellants, however, submit that the prohibition affects them in
a particular manner, since its effect is to prevent them from installing a
succah in order to practice what they consider to be a religious rite. We
should, however, note that the prohibition has the same effect on the other
co-owners with religious beliefs, in that it also prevents them from installing
any object associated with their religious practice on their balcony, porch or
patio, be it a cross, a statue of the Virgin Mary, a Buddhist altar, a Tibetan
prayer wheel, etc.

[
138
]

Nor do I believe that it is possible to support the argument that
the restrictions affect the Jewish orthodox co-owners differently than other believers
because they are the only ones who believe they have an obligation to construct
a succah on their balcony. It cannot be maintained that persons of another
faith do not wish just as sincerely as the Orthodox Jews to express their
beliefs and perform their rites by constructing on their balconies or patios.
As the appellants rightly submit, it does not fall to the courts to rule on the
correct interpretation of religious precepts. Nor, I would add, is it their
place to rank the beliefs held by different persons.

[
139
]

Is it possible, then, to argue that the impugned clauses have an
adverse effect on the co-owners with religious beliefs, but not on those
without?

[
140
]

The answer is no. Non-believers also enjoy rights under
section 3
of
the
Charter
, notably, freedom of conscience and freedom of opinion. If
exposed to religious symbols, they too would have the right to express their
lack of observance of religious doctrine by installing a sign or a banner or by
any other means. In
R. v. Big M. Drug Mart Ltd.
,
[54]
the Supreme Court recognized that freedom
of conscience included freedom of expression and the manifestation of
non-belief in religion.

[
141
]

What is more, not only are believers and non-believers affected
equally, so are co-owners who wish to manifest their political or social
convictions by setting up banners, electoral signs, flags, etc. during an
election or referendum period, for example.

[
142
]

Co-owners may also wish to exercise their freedom of expression by
placing posters on their balconies to demonstrate their dissatisfaction with
the services of their insurance company or city, a right protected by
section 3

of the
Charter
as well as by
section 2(
b
) of the
Canadian
Charter
, as recently affirmed by the Supreme Court in
R. v. Guignard
.
[55]

[
143
]

To sum up, in my opinion the impugned clauses are not discriminatory
within the meaning of
section 10
of the
Charter
, as they affect all
co-owners equally with respect to their fundamental freedoms within the meaning
of
section 3
of the
Charter
by prohibiting any construction that would
be necessary or useful to the expression of their beliefs, convictions or
opinions, whatever they may be.

[
144
]

On the contrary, they reflect a compromise whereby all co-owners,
because they desire to live in co-ownership with hundreds of other people in an
environment that obliges proximity, waive the use of the balconies, porches or
patios adjacent to their apartments for the exercise of their rights under

section 3
of the
Charter
, without distinction, exclusion or preference
with respect to one fundamental freedom over another.

Distinction on prohibited ground

[
145
]

The common element linking the prohibited grounds listed in
section
10
of the
Charter
is that they are all personal characteristics.

[
146
]

If I had concluded that the effect of the impugned clauses were to
create a distinction with respect to the appellants, I would have found that
the distinction was based on a prohibited ground, in this case,
"religion".

Impairment of the right to full and
equal recognition of a
Charter
-protected right or freedom

[
147
]

As this Court noted in
Quebec (A.G.) v. Lambert
, cited above,
at para. 79, "
It is the most crucial factor. It
involves two notions: the prejudice suffered and the infringement of human
dignity
."

[
148
]

According to the appellants, the prejudice suffered consists of an
infringement on their freedom of religion because they were prevented from
setting up a succah on their terrace.

[
149
]

The Supreme Court has stated that "
[
t]he essence of the concept of freedom of
religion is the right to entertain such religious beliefs as a person chooses,
the right to declare religious beliefs openly and without fear of hindrance or
reprisal, and the right to manifest religious belief by worship and practice or
by teaching and dissemination.
"
[56]
In short, the freedom of religion that is
protected by
section 3
of the
Charter
includes the right to express
religious beliefs and to practise the associated rites.

[
150
]

That said, there is discrimination and a duty to accommodate only
when the rite is more than simply an act that the believer would like to
practise or that would give him or her pleasure. Rather, it must be a precept
that the person sincerely believes must be fulfilled in order to remain true to
his or her beliefs.

[
151
]

In
R. v. Edwards
,
[57]
a
majority of the Supreme Court recognized that the
Ontario
Retail Business
Holidays Act
negatively affected Jewish persons and Seventh-day Adventists
for whom "
it is a religious tenet …
not to work or transact business on Saturdays
" but, with respect to Hindus,
found "
that there is no religious prohibition
enjoining adherents from working on Wednesdays, but that there exists some
moral obligation to pray on that day
."

[
152
]

This implies that those who allege discrimination must adduce
sufficient evidence to establish that they see themselves as being forced to
choose between respecting the impugned clauses and respecting a religious
precept.

[
153
]

This was the task the appellants undertook before the trial judge.
Even if it did not fall to him to determine which of the two rabbis best
described the content of Jewish beliefs regarding Succot, after analyzing the
evidence as a whole, and most particularly the conduct of the appellants before
and after they acquired an apartment at the Sanctuaire,
[58]
I cannot conclude that he erred in finding
that the appellants did not have a religious obligation to set up a succah on
their balcony, patio or porch during Succot. Rather, it was an act that they
wished to carry out in 1996 and 1997 to discharge a moral obligation to
celebrate Succot. This is a finding of fact made by the trial judge that is
supported by the evidence, independently of the debate between the two rabbis.

[
154
]

There is therefore no evidence of prejudice suffered by the
appellants with respect to their
Charter
-protected right to freedom of
religion.

[
155
]

Finally, since the matter before us involves equality rights, we
must recall that a difference in treatment, when it exists, is discriminatory
only if it has the effect of making the persons discriminated against less
worthy of recognition or value as human beings.
[59]

[
156
]

In my view, I cannot see how the prohibition against setting up
succahs, crucifixes, statues, altars, etc. on their balconies, patios or
porches belittles the worth of the appellants or perpetuates prejudices against
them.

- -
- - - - -

[
157
]

As the appellants have not established that their contract with the
other co-owners contains discriminatory clauses within the meaning of
section
10
of the
Charter
, I can see no need to determine whether the other
co-owners, represented by the syndicate, had a duty to accommodate and whether
the offer of a communal succah was an appropriate measure in the circumstances,
as the trial judge and the representatives of the Canadian Jewish Congress
concluded.

[
158
]

I shall conclude the
Charter
part of the analysis by
mentioning that
section 9.1
of the
Charter
is not applicable to
contractual matters to which
sections 13
and
10
of the
Charter
apply. In
fact,
section 9.1
is relevant only to establish the precise scope of the
fundamental rights and freedoms set out in
sections 1
to
9
of the
Charter
.
[60]
Once the analysis of sections 13 and 10
are complete, if the court concludes that there is discrimination with respect
to the recognition and exercise of a fundamental right, as defined, this
discrimination cannot subsequently be justified under
section 9.1
.
[61]
Discrimination having been established,
the contractual clause at issue is declared to be without effect or, at the
very least, as giving rise to a duty to accommodate.
[62]

[
159
]

Thus, in employment law (
section 16
of the
Charter
),
discrimination is forbidden in general. The only exceptions are set out in the
Charter

itself, in the provisions following
section 16
, and they include justified
professional requirements and requirements related to the characteristics of
certain employers (
section 20
). Other exceptions to equality rights cannot be
created by applying section 9.1.

IV.
The right to an injunction and

article 1080
C.C.Q.

[
160
]

Section 1080 C.C.Q. remains to be discussed. Like my colleague
Justice Morin and the trial judge, I find that this provision does not restrict
the cases where an injunction may be ordered. Indeed, in my view, this article
accomplishes two things.

[
161
]

First, it confers the right to an injunction not only on the
co-owner who is the victim of a contractual breach, but also on the syndicate
representing all the co-owners, including the one who refuses to comply. In
short, when a co-owner's refusal to comply with the declaration appears to
cause serious and irreparable prejudice—two familiar concepts that are also
referred to in article 752 C.C.P—article 1080 C.C.Q. recognizes the interest
that the two different parties may have in seeking the contractual remedy of
specific performance. This reflects the collective nature of the contract
(article 1010 C.C.Q.)
[63]
and,
like 1079 C.C.Q., forestalls any debate as to who has a legal interest.

[
162
]

Finally, it provides that, in the event of a violation of the order
issued, the syndicate or the co-owner who obtained the injunction may request,
in addition to a conviction for contempt of court, an order of expropriation of
the co-owner at fault, which would put an end to any possibility of violating
the declaration.

- -
- - - - -

[
163
]

For these reasons, I would, like my colleague Justice Morin, dismiss
the appeals with costs.

REASONS OF JUSTICE BAUDOUIN

I have had the opportunity to read the opinions of my colleagues
Justices Benoît Morin and Pierre Dalphond and, like them, I would dismiss the
two appeals with costs.

[
165
]

I concur with the reasons of my colleague Justice Pierre Dalphond.
The restrictions that were reasonably imposed by the declaration of co-ownership
in the interest of all are in no way discriminatory against the appellants.
They affect all co-owners equally and are part of what they must voluntarily
accept as a reasonable limit on their rights for the general benefit of all and
for the common good.

[
166
]

Moreover, I would add that even if the problem were addressed from
the much narrower perspective of the judicial review of public normative texts
(which I refrain from doing), I cannot see how my colleague Justice Morin's
application of the criteria set out by the Supreme Court could in any way lead
to a conclusion other than the outright dismissal of the two appeals.
